Hope for farmers II

By: Tarryn Crossman | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We go back to two farmers who had nothing but hope this time last year

Summary:
Recap story with the farmers from 'Hope for Farmers'
story of how the drought has lifted for them

Further information:
VO and visuals from the previous story
In February 2016 we brought you the heart breaking story of two farmers whose lives were almost destroyed by the drought that ripped through South Africa.
Oom Jim has a cattle farm in Bray in the Kalahari. When I arrived on his farm last February They had only received a total of …. In …. Months and it was heart breaking to see the state of the cattle.

Up sound from the previous piece
Choosing which cows to kill section

Derek link on a farm? Or VO with visuals
Michris and his family live in Bultfontien by the time to arrived to interview him in February he was a broken man

Up sound from previous piece
Crying about how this has destroyed them and they may not be able to ever come back from it

VO and visuals from the piece
Every evening Michris took his family up to a rock that over looked their farm to pray for rain. He knew his first crop was already underdeveloped, but all they had left was hope.

Up sound from the previous piece
Michris what they need to survive – the section on hope

Link with Derek on a farm or vo with visuals:
The drought has not lifted all over South Africa and some areas like …. are currently sitting with severe water shortages, but in Bultfontien Michris and the surrounding farmers have received …. ml more than than they did this time last year. We went back to see exactly what has happened with Michris and his family since the 2016 drought that nearly took their farm and their lively hood.

Michris walking through his fields
• Is this the same fields we were in this time last year?
• What has changed?
• Does this mean the drought is over for you and these farmers?
• What got you through?
• What did you learn from the 2016 drought?

Link with Derek on a farm or vo with visuals:
445km away in the town of Bray in the Kalahari Oom Jim’s story of hope will restore your faith in Humanity.

Oom Jim in a field full of fat cows:
1. After we left last last year you had started to receive food for the cattle from various donors. Can you tell us what happened after we left? What got you through the 2016 drought?
Success story of the food that was donated and driven out to Bray. The farmers who offered to look after some of Oom Jims cattle. Video footage from previous insert and from the family
2. Where are you today as we sit here? – Drought has lifted, the dams are filling up as the river is running for the first time in 10 years
“The cattle are fat and we will start again” Oom Jim
3. What did you learn from the drought of 2016 – about humanity?

Possible link in studio about the fact that the drought may not be over in the whole of South Africa, but ….. ???

Press Release:


Farmers Update
The new year is already delivering good news: rain has fallen in many drought-stricken areas and healthy crops are returning the smiles to the faces of desperate farmers. In 2016 Oom Jim Botha and Michris Janse Van Rensburg’s livelihoods were devastated by the drought. But, it seems things are looking up. Carte Blanche revisits the farmers whose desperate prayers for rain seem to have brought back the water, crops and herds.


Script:


Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
1 00:00 Opening with Michris and wife praying on a hill Intro music

Michris: Thank you for the abundant rain that you gave us. We needed it so badly; we also want to ask you to please send rain where there is still drought across the country. Amen
2 00:26 Michris and windmill Michris: The last time you guys where here it looked like Afghanistan and now it look like England.
3 00:36 Oom Jim via Skype with Derek Jim: Derek, the most difficult thing for me was the day I had to take my rifle and shoot three cows that were too weak and might not live longer. But now things have change and yes, now we can almost cry tears of joy because the cattle that have survived are beautiful, they’re fat even feeding them in a feedlot, wouldn’t have made them this fat. So yes, we believe things will get better.
4 01:14 Derek Derek: At the beginning of last year we brought you the heart breaking story of 2 famers whose lives were almost destroyed by South Africa’s wide spread drought.
5 01:28 V/O introduction of Mnikeli V/O: Mnikeli Ndabambi is the general manager of operations at weather SA.
6 01:33 Mnikeli Ndabambi Mnikeli: The drought of 2015 that went over to 2016 was actually the most severe drought since 1900.
7 01:45 Footage of 2015 drought.

V/O V/O: Oom Jim Botha has a cattle farm in the Bray in Kalahari, when I arrived at his farm last year they were putting out their last two bales of hail to feed their cattle.
9 02:00 Madeline Botha Madeline: They just lie here then they wait for us to put out the bale because there is no more grass for them inside of the field

10 02:08 Madeline Botha speaks to camera with cows in the background So what happens is the stronger ones they eat first because they can push the weaker ones away
Five already died because they couldn’t even walk from the tree up to here where we feed them.
11 02:23 Madeline Botha speaks over images of cows 12feeding and some loosing weight. Jim Both joins as they look at the dying cows It’s bad seeing the weak ones dying in there. And you have to decide and its not their fault so if you have to decide (cries) that’s what makes it difficult because who do you help? Do you help your strong cows or do you help the weak ones? Which one do you help?
12 03:01 Derek V/O introducing Michris V/O: Michris Jansen van Rensburg and his family live here in Bulfontein in the Freestaste, when we arrived to interview him a year ago all he had left was hope.
13 03:12 Michris interview with Derek from February 2015 Michris: We know as a famer you handle I would say your best time planting is 20 November to 5 December for maize. Every night when I see the date on the bible 26 December and 27 December, 2nd of January I realize I didn’t plant yet. I think most famers are scared that one day they are not going to be famers and their family, their kids will say 2015 drought destroyed us.
14 03:49 Derek in the fields Derek: We have returned to the farm lands exactly a year later to find out how for Michris and Oom Jim the drought has lifted
15 03:58 Driving shots of Derek and the land as they visit Michris
16 04:07 Michris interview in the fields with Derek Derek: Michris we were here round about the same time last year its so difficult to believe that this is the same field.
Michris: Its unbelievable the difference that rain makes for faith and us to plant again. We are grateful that’s all we can say.
Derek: Last year I would say about 20% of your normal production?
Michris: Yes definitely we only planted about 20% of our maize but this year we planted, at this moment every corner we could have
Derek: so looking ahead at the rest of this season, what’s in store?
Michris: After this lovely rain we got now in January I can, I’m positive.
Derek: you are smiling a lot more.
Michris: yes, how can a farmer not smile if he sees beautiful maize like this?
17 05:02 Derek linking to Oom Jim Derek: around 50km away in the town of Bray in the Kalahari, Oom Jim story of survival will restore your faith in humanity.
18 05:11 Oom Jim on Skype Jim: Since the last time you were here, after the programme, we received a lot of help. People phoned from all over, some of my friends phoned, guys that are in the same industry as I am. On guy phoned me and said ‘Jim, I couldn’t sleep that night” the next morning he sent a truck with a trailer filled with feed. Someone phone me while I was driving next to my cattle and we spoke about the drought and about the programme and the next moment he asked me ‘ Can I please pray for you?’ I never would have thought that there still are some many people out there that care about another. But with the grace from above, it has started raining again. Last season we only had 216. Rain in Molopo in total and now, in January alone we have already had 128mm rain.
19 06:25 Derek interview with Mnikeli Derek: In some parts of the country people are saying that the drought has lifted, can we be that optimistic?
Mnikeli: Derek I can see some people are already smiling and saying the drought is over. The thing is the drought has been too serve yes for Agriculture because of the recent rains that were coming from the tropics most people have experienced more especially the eastern half of country they have been coming down slowly so there is a bit of relief in terms of the agricultural drought but then the data is not enough to say that with confidence. We also have your hydrological drought which is more like your water related looking at the dams now, the Vaal dam which has increased up to about 60% this time of the year although the other dams in the East have not reached 60% they have increased in terms of the dam levels and most of them are above 40% which is good news but I think in terms of water management we still need to be conscious we need to have that awareness that we must use water with care because now we are going to get into winter so these areas that we are mentioning in the Eastern part of the country there are summer rain fall areas so we are going with winter the dam levels are averaging at 50% and below so we must really look after the way we use water.
20 07:59 Derek with Michris on the field Derek: Michris what have you learnt through this drought?
Michris: I think to instil hope all the time. I almost got to a point where said I cain’t take this anymore this is too much but for my family side my son which I want him to farm I get my faith and continue and try again.
21 08:32 Jim Skype Jim: what I’ve learned from this drought is that you have to think ahead. If it happens again I’ll do things differently. I’ll immediately pick my main flock and then I’ll sell the rest of my cattle. Rather start from the beginning afterwards, from the bottom that’s basically what I’m going now. I think we’re safe now and we’ll make it going forward.
